claims.text: The official Node release schedule is maintained by the Node.js Release WG in github.com/nodejs/Release (schedule.json and README 'Release schedule'); nodejs.org/en/about/previous-releases links to it. Retrieved via WebFetch (output was summarized by a fetch model, not raw bytes).
Node 24: start 2025-05-06; Active LTS 2025-10-28; Maintenance 2026-10-20; end-of-life 2028-04-30. So on 2026-10-17 it is still Active LTS, moving to Maintenance 3 days later.

Node 26: released 2026-05-05; scheduled LTS date 2026-10-28; Maintenance 2027-10-20; EOL 2029-04-30. As of 2026-10-17 it is NOT yet LTS (still Current); LTS begins in 11 days per schedule. previous-releases page lists v26 as 'Current'.
Node 22: start 2024-04-24; Active LTS 2024-10-29; Maintenance 2025-10-21; EOL 2027-04-30. As of 2026-10-17 it is Maintenance LTS (supported, critical fixes/security only), not EOL.

Recommendation for a deployment requiring LTS today (2026-10-17): choose Node 24. It is Active LTS now and supported to 2028-04-30. Node 26 is not LTS until 2026-10-28; reconsider migrating to 26 after that date, once its LTS release is actually published and your dependencies are tested.

evidence.locator: text: production apps should use Active or Maintenance LTS

claims.text: The schedule gives planned phase dates only. It does not prove which patch version is installed, that it contains the latest security fixes, or that a distro/container image has backported them. Verify with `node -v`, the official security/release announcements and the image/package provenance. Schedule dates can change; also the previous-releases table's date column appears to be 'last updated' (patch dates), not EOL dates, so do not read it as the schedule.

evidence.locator: table column note and LTS text

recommendation: Deploy Node 24 now (latest 24.x patch, pinned and verified). Plan evaluation of Node 26 after its scheduled LTS date 2026-10-28. Avoid new deployments on Node 22 (Maintenance, EOL 2027-04-30) and do not use 25 (EOL).
